subject: Python
text: Order.. matters.. And in Python, lists make it easy to work with ordered data. Lists are

subject: Python
text: a built-in data structure for storing and accessing objects which belong in a specific

subject: Python
text: sequence. We will now learn how to create and use lists, and we will do so in a linear

subject: Python
text: and orderly fashion...

subject: Python
text: There are two ways to create a list. One way

subject: Python
text: is to use the list constructor. But a simpler and more common way is to use brackets.

subject: Python
text: When creating a list, you can also pre-populate it with values. For example, let’s create

subject: Python
text: a list with the first few prime numbers.

subject: Python
text: You can always add values later by using the “append” method which allows you to add

subject: Python
text: new values to the end of the list. Let’s append the next two prime numbers: 17… and

subject: Python
text: If you display the list, you will see it contains the new values. Notice how lists preserve

subject: Python
text: the order of the data - this is different from sets. In sets, the order is not important.

subject: Python
text: In lists, order is everything. You do not have to view the entire list. If

subject: Python
text: you want to see a specific value, you can access it by its index. In computer science,

subject: Python
text: you start counting with 0, not 1. So the elements in our list “primes” are indexed 0.. 1..

subject: Python
text: 2.. 3.. 4.. 5.. 6.. and 7.. To view the first item, you type the name

subject: Python
text: of the list, and the index in brackets. The first item is 2.

subject: Python
text: The second item has index 1, and the second item is 3.

subject: Python
text: And so on…

subject: Python
text: Notice how the indices increase by one as you go from left to right.

subject: Python
text: And they decrease by one when you go from right to left.

subject: Python
text: When you get to the beginning, the index is 0. If you decrease the index once more, you

subject: Python
text: get -1. Here, Python wraps back around to the end of the list. So the last item is -1,

subject: Python
text: the next to last is -2, and so on. This is convenient when you want to look at

subject: Python
text: the values at the end of a list. The last item is 19…

subject: Python
text: The next to last prime is 17…

subject: Python
text: And we reach the beginning of the list with index -8.

subject: Python
text: Be careful - you can only wrap around once. If you try to find the value of index -9,

subject: Python
text: you get an index error.

subject: Python
text: Another way to access values in a list is

subject: Python
text: by slicing. This lets you retrieve a range of values from your list.

subject: Python
text: We will continue to use our list of primes.

subject: Python
text: To slice this list, type the name of the list, bracket, a starting index, a colon, a stopping

subject: Python
text: index, then a closing bracket… The result is a sublist that starts at index 2, and continues

subject: Python
text: until it reaches index 5. Be careful. Slicing includes the value at the starting index,

subject: Python
text: but excludes the stopping index. The beginning value is included; the ending value is not.

subject: Python
text: One more slice… This will start at the beginning, which is index 0, and continue to index 6,

subject: Python
text: which is 17. It will not include the final number, so this slice includes the primes

subject: Python
text: from 2 through 13.

subject: Python
text: Lists can contain more than prime numbers.

subject: Python
text: They can contain integers…booleans… strings… floats… and even other lists.

subject: Python
text: Many languages require lists to contain values of the same type, but not Python. With Python,

subject: Python
text: you are free to insert multiple data types in the same list.

subject: Python
text: Lists can also contain duplicate values. Here is another way lists are different from sets.

subject: Python
text: For example, suppose you want to record the numbers you roll on a pair of dice. Pretend

subject: Python
text: you roll a 4.. 7.. 2.. 7.. 12.. 4 and 7.. If you look at the list, all the values are

subject: Python
text: there, even the repeated rolls.

subject: Python
text: You can also combine lists. To see how, create

subject: Python
text: two separate lists: A list of numbers…

subject: Python
text: And a list of letters… To combine these two lists into a single list,

subject: Python
text: use the plus sign. Numbers + letters equals 1, 2, 3 .. a, b, c...

subject: Python
text: But order matters. If you reverse this and

subject: Python
text: compute letters + numbers you get a, b, c.. 1, 2, 3..

subject: Python
text: Combining lists is called “concatenation”.

subject: Python
text: Observe. The list of numbers..

subject: Python
text: and the list of letters are unchanged.

subject: Python
text: There are many other methods for working with

subject: Python
text: lists. To see them all, pass any list to the directory function.

subject: Python
text: To learn how to use one of these methods, use the help function. For example, there

subject: Python
text: is a method for reversing a list. The help text gives full details on what it does and

subject: Python
text: how to use it.

subject: Python
text: Lists start at 0 and end… ... they end precisely

subject: Python
text: when you are finished. You can slice them… You can concatenate them… You can reverse

subject: Python
text: them… You can even clear them… If I were to make a list of all the uses of lists, I
